title: fix(backend): create DB export temp paths with mkdtemp instead of predictable timestamps
body:
## Summary
The DB backup export routes build a deterministic path under the shared, world-writable `os.tmpdir()` (one with second-granularity, one with millisecond-granularity) without `mkdtemp`, `O_EXCL`, or any random component before writing the exported database backup there. On a multi-user or multi-tenant host, a local unprivileged process that predicts or races the path can pre-place a symlink to redirect where the plaintext backup is written or read from.

## Evidence
- `src/app/api/db-backups/exportAll/route.ts:31-36` — `path.join(os.tmpdir(), \`omniroute-export-${timestamp}\`)`, `timestamp` at second granularity.
- `src/app/api/db-backups/export/route.ts:28-35` — same pattern at millisecond granularity.
- Both call `mkdirSync`/write directly into the resulting path without an exclusive-creation flag or a `crypto.randomBytes`-derived component.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/src/app/api/db-backups/exportAll/route.ts#L31-L36

## Why this matters
This is a classic TOCTOU/symlink temp-file weakness. It is not remotely exploitable and does not apply to the common single-user Electron/desktop deployment, but this project explicitly documents and supports multi-tenant Docker/VPS deployment (`scripts/vps/`), where a co-located, lower-privileged local process predicting or racing this path is a realistic scenario.

## Attack or failure scenario
On a shared VPS/container host running OmniRoute alongside other locally-executing processes, a local unprivileged actor pre-creates a symlink at the predictable `omniroute-export-<timestamp>` path (racing the narrow, but non-zero, window and/or the coarser second-granularity variant) pointing at a file outside the intended temp scope. When the export route writes the backup, it follows the symlink, potentially overwriting an unintended file or exposing the backup's contents at an attacker-chosen location.

## Root cause
Deterministic, non-exclusive path construction under a shared temp directory instead of `fs.mkdtempSync`/`O_EXCL`-based exclusive creation.

## Recommended fix
Use `fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "omniroute-export-"))` (which appends a random suffix and guarantees exclusive creation) in both routes instead of manually constructing a timestamp-based path.

## Acceptance criteria
- Both export routes create their temporary working directory via an exclusive, randomized mechanism (`mkdtemp` or equivalent) rather than a predictable timestamp-based name.

## Suggested labels
bug, backend

## Priority
P3

## Severity
Low — requires local access to a shared/multi-tenant host; does not apply to the primary single-user desktop use case.

## Confidence
Confirmed — verified the exact path-construction code in both routes lacks any exclusive/random component.

title: fix(docker): cliproxyapi sidecar published on 0.0.0.0 with no auth configuration (opt-in profile)

labels.name: docker
labels.description: Pull requests that update docker code

body:
## Summary
The optional `cliproxyapi` Docker Compose sidecar (profile `cliproxyapi`) is explicitly configured with `HOST=0.0.0.0` and published on the host with no host-IP scoping. No API key or auth-related environment variable is passed to it anywhere in the compose service definition, and there is no comment flagging this as requiring external network isolation, unlike the same file's Redis service.

## Evidence
- `docker-compose.yml:284-303` (service `cliproxyapi`, profile `cliproxyapi`):
  - `environment: - PORT=${CLIPROXYAPI_PORT:-8317} - HOST=0.0.0.0` — only these two variables are set; no auth token, API key, or credential variable appears anywhere in the block.
  - `ports: - "${CLIPROXYAPI_PORT:-8317}:${CLIPROXYAPI_PORT:-8317}"` — no host-IP prefix, so this publishes to all interfaces by default (the same pattern as the primary app-exposure finding filed in this audit).
- The image (`docker.io/eceasy/cli-proxy-api:v6.9.7`) is a third-party, closed-source binary; whether it enforces its own internal auth independent of this compose configuration could not be verified from this repository's source and is called out below as the residual unknown.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/docker-compose.yml#L284-L303

## Why this matters
This sidecar is opt-in (gated behind the `cliproxyapi` profile, off by default), which lowers the severity relative to the default-exposure finding filed alongside this one — but an operator who enables it to integrate CLIProxyAPI gets the same "published on every interface with no visible auth" pattern this repo already recognized as risky enough to fix for Redis, without the same fix or warning applied here.

## Attack or failure scenario
An operator enables the `cliproxyapi` profile on a host reachable from a LAN or the internet. If the underlying `eceasy/cli-proxy-api` binary does not enforce its own authentication by default (unverified from this repo alone), anyone who can reach the published port gets unauthenticated access to whatever this sidecar proxies — potentially provider credentials or LLM call routing.

## Root cause
Same class as the primary compose-exposure finding: the port is published without host-IP scoping and without an explicit auth requirement being surfaced in the compose configuration or documentation, leaving the effective security posture entirely dependent on an unverified third-party binary's own defaults.

## Recommended fix
Bind this service's port to `127.0.0.1` by default (matching the Redis precedent), and document (or better, wire in via a compose environment variable if the image supports it) how to configure the underlying binary's authentication before recommending it be exposed beyond loopback.

## Acceptance criteria
- The `cliproxyapi` service's published port defaults to loopback-only unless the operator explicitly opts into a non-loopback bind.
- Documentation states whether/how to configure authentication on the underlying `eceasy/cli-proxy-api` image, resolving the current unknown.

## Suggested labels
docker

## Priority
P2

## Severity
Low-Medium — opt-in profile lowers likelihood; unverified whether the third-party binary has its own auth layer, so actual impact needs confirmation from the image's own documentation.

## Confidence
Needs verification — the compose-level configuration (0.0.0.0 bind, no auth env var) is confirmed by direct inspection, but whether `eceasy/cli-proxy-api:v6.9.7` enforces its own default authentication is outside this repository's source and was not independently verified.

title: fix(resilience): unbounded in-memory buffering in HuggingChat NDJSON executor — no size cap or timeout

labels.name: backlog
labels.description: Tracked for future work; not blocking

body:
## Summary
The HuggingChat NDJSON executor accumulates the entire upstream response into memory with no byte cap and no timeout, relying entirely on the upstream service eventually emitting a terminal marker or closing the connection. A slow, hostile, or malfunctioning HuggingChat backend can drive unbounded memory growth per in-flight request.

## Evidence
- `open-sse/executors/huggingchat/jsonlStream.ts:40-177` (`streamJsonlToOpenAi`) and `:179-221` (`readJsonlResponse`) — both accumulate `buffer`/`fullText` from the upstream `ReadableStream` with no maximum size check and no `AbortSignal.timeout` anywhere in the read loop; termination depends entirely on the upstream emitting `finalAnswer`/`status:finished` or closing the stream on its own.
- This is a distinct file/mechanism from the two already-tracked, adjacent memory-bounding efforts: #12284 ("bound in-memory caches... in SSE streaming and executors") enumerates specific caches (Adapta/GigaChat/browser-pool/ZCode buffer) that do not include this file, and #12420 covers call-log artifact size limits, a different buffer entirely.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/open-sse/executors/huggingchat/jsonlStream.ts#L40

## Why this matters
Every other executor in this pipeline handles a request against a real, rate-limited LLM provider; a proxy that fans out to many concurrent requests against a backend with no per-request memory ceiling is exposed to a straightforward resource-exhaustion condition if that backend ever stalls, loops, or is itself compromised/hostile — a single slow or malicious upstream response can grow unbounded and, at sufficient concurrency, exhaust process memory.

## Attack or failure scenario
The HuggingChat backend (third-party, outside OmniRoute's control) stalls mid-response or streams an unbounded amount of NDJSON without ever emitting a terminal marker, whether due to a backend bug or a compromised/malicious HuggingChat-compatible endpoint an operator has pointed this executor at. Each such in-flight request accumulates memory indefinitely; enough concurrent requests exhaust the process's memory budget, degrading or crashing the OmniRoute instance for all tenants.

## Root cause
The read loop's termination condition is purely upstream-driven (a specific JSON field or stream closure) with no independent resource ceiling (max bytes, max duration) enforced by the consuming code.

## Recommended fix
Add a maximum accumulated-byte ceiling and an `AbortSignal.timeout` (or equivalent) to both `streamJsonlToOpenAi` and `readJsonlResponse`, aborting and surfacing a clear upstream-error response if either limit is exceeded — matching the bounding pattern issue #12284 is already applying to the other named caches/buffers in this same executor layer.

## Acceptance criteria
- Both functions abort and return a clear error (rather than growing memory unboundedly) when the upstream response exceeds a defined size or duration limit.
- A test simulates a stalled/never-terminating upstream stream and confirms the request is aborted rather than hanging or growing memory indefinitely.

## Suggested labels
bug, backend, resilience

## Priority
P2

## Severity
Medium — single-request/single-tenant denial-of-service risk, not a cross-tenant data exposure.

## Confidence
Confirmed — read both functions' full read loops; no size cap or timeout present in either.

title: feat(docker): pin exact versions of the four AI CLIs in the runner-cli stage

labels.name: dependencies
labels.description: Pull requests that update a dependency file

labels.name: docker
labels.description: Pull requests that update docker code

body:
## Summary
The `runner-cli` Dockerfile stage installs four AI coding-agent CLIs globally with no version pins, meaning every image rebuild silently pulls whatever each package's `latest` tag currently resolves to, with no lockfile, checksum, or `--ignore-scripts` protection, for tools that get filesystem, shell, and (per the docker-socket finding filed alongside this one) Docker-daemon access.

## Evidence
- `Dockerfile:348`: `npm install -g --no-audit --no-fund @openai/codex @anthropic-ai/claude-code droid openclaw@latest` — no version specified for `@openai/codex`, `@anthropic-ai/claude-code`, or `droid`; `openclaw` explicitly pins to `@latest`.
- This `runner-cli` stage is the build target consumed by `docker-compose.yml`'s `omniroute-cli` service and by `docker-compose.prod.yml:53`, so it reaches a production-labeled compose file, not only a local dev convenience image.
- This install is outside the coverage of both Trivy (scans installed package versions at a point in time, not install-time integrity of a floating tag) and Socket's `projectIgnorePaths` configuration (doesn't cover ad hoc `npm install -g` calls inside a Dockerfile `RUN` step).

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/Dockerfile#L348

## Why this matters
An unpinned `npm install -g` in a Dockerfile means the exact code that ends up in every built image is decided by the npm registry at build time, not by anything reviewed or committed in this repository. Combined with the elevated access these specific tools already have in the `omniroute-cli` container (shell execution, Docker socket in some configurations), a compromised publish of any of the four packages reaches production images automatically on the next rebuild, with no diff for anyone to review.

## Attack or failure scenario
A supply-chain compromise of any of the four upstream packages (compromised maintainer account, malicious dependency-confusion publish, or a build-time postinstall script) ships in its next `latest`/unpinned release. The next `docker build` of the `runner-cli` stage — whether a scheduled rebuild, a release pipeline run, or a developer's local build — pulls the compromised version with no version-pin mismatch to flag it, and no lockfile diff for review to catch it before the image ships.

## Root cause
Global `npm install -g` inside a Dockerfile bypasses the project's own lockfile discipline (`package-lock.json` exists and is used for the app's own dependencies) entirely for these four packages.

## Recommended fix
Pin explicit versions for all four packages (`@openai/codex@X.Y.Z`, `@anthropic-ai/claude-code@X.Y.Z`, `droid@X.Y.Z`, `openclaw@X.Y.Z`) and update them via a deliberate, reviewed bump (ideally with the same Dependabot/Renovate-style process, if one exists, used for the rest of the dependency tree) rather than tracking `latest` implicitly on every rebuild.

## Acceptance criteria
- `Dockerfile:348` (or wherever this line moves to) specifies an exact version for each of the four packages.
- A documented process (or automation) exists for deliberately bumping these pins, rather than leaving them to float.

## Suggested labels
dependencies, docker

## Priority
P2

## Severity
Medium — not independently exploitable without a compromised upstream package, but removes the last line of defense (pinning) against exactly that class of supply-chain attack for tools with elevated container access.

## Confidence
Confirmed — verified the exact Dockerfile line and traced which compose files/stages consume the `runner-cli` target.

title: docs(dependencies): state that socket.yml is a registry-side post-publish scan, not a CI gate

labels.name: dependencies
labels.description: Pull requests that update a dependency file

labels.name: backlog
labels.description: Tracked for future work; not blocking

body:
## Summary
`socket.yml` and the surrounding Socket.dev documentation (`SECURITY.md`, `docs/security/SOCKET_DEV_FINDINGS.md`) present what reads like an enforced supply-chain scanning pipeline, but no GitHub Actions workflow, `package.json` script, or `Makefile` target actually invokes Socket.dev — the config only shapes ignore-paths for Socket's own external, registry-side scan of the published npm package, and is not a gate on PRs, merges, or releases in this repository.

## Evidence
- `socket.yml` present at repo root, version 2, with a detailed `projectIgnorePaths` configuration.
- `grep -rn "socket" .github/workflows/*.yml package.json Makefile` (excluding unrelated matches like `net.Socket`/`websocket`) returns no reference to Socket.dev, `socketsecurity`, or any Socket CLI/action invocation.
- The maintainer stated directly on issue #7212 that Socket.dev integration is "out of scope... if you want to add Socket.dev scanning to your fork, the standard GitHub Action marketplace has Socket Security actions" — confirming this is a known, accepted gap rather than an oversight, but the surrounding documentation (`SECURITY.md`, `docs/security/SOCKET_DEV_FINDINGS.md`) does not make that limitation clear to a reader who encounters `socket.yml` and assumes it's wired into CI.
- Issue #2863 (a real Socket.dev finding that led to a v3.8.6 fix) confirms Socket *did* flag something real for this project — via its external, registry-side scan of the published package, not a repo-side gate.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/socket.yml

## Why this matters
A supply-chain-scanning config file that isn't wired into CI provides no protection against a malicious or compromised dependency landing in a PR before release — the only backstop is Socket's own external scan of the already-published npm package, which fires after the fact (as it did for #2863). Given this repository's explicit investment in supply-chain hygiene elsewhere (`.gitleaks.toml`, `.trivyignore`, `.zizmor.yml`), this is a gap in an otherwise deliberately hardened area, and the documentation's framing could give maintainers/contributors false confidence that dependency changes are being scanned pre-merge when they are not.

## Attack or failure scenario
A malicious dependency version (typosquat, compromised maintainer account, or a subtly backdoored transitive update) is introduced via a routine dependency-bump PR. Nothing in CI runs Socket.dev (or an equivalent) against the changed dependency tree before merge; the only chance of catching it is Socket's own after-the-fact scan of the next published release, or another tool (Trivy, gitleaks) catching an unrelated symptom.

## Root cause
`socket.yml`'s presence and the accompanying documentation imply an enforced pipeline that does not exist in this repository; the actual protection is an external, asynchronous, post-publish scan the maintainer has explicitly decided not to replicate as a repo-side CI gate.

## Recommended fix
Either wire a Socket Security GitHub Action (or equivalent open-source supply-chain scanner already compatible with this repo's stack — e.g. extending the existing `.trivyignore`/Trivy setup to cover dependency CVEs pre-merge) into a workflow that runs on dependency-changing PRs, or update `SECURITY.md`/`docs/security/SOCKET_DEV_FINDINGS.md` to state plainly that `socket.yml` governs only the external post-publish scan and is not a CI gate, so the documentation matches reality.

## Acceptance criteria
- Either a CI workflow demonstrably invokes dependency/supply-chain scanning gated on PR merge, or the security documentation is corrected to accurately describe `socket.yml`'s actual (external, post-publish, non-blocking) scope.

## Suggested labels
security (label does not exist on this repo — nearest available: documentation), documentation, dependencies

## Priority
P2

## Severity
Medium — no active exploit, but a real gap in pre-merge supply-chain defense and a documentation-vs-reality mismatch in a security-sensitive area.

## Confidence
Confirmed — maintainer's own statement on #7212 plus direct grep confirming no workflow invokes Socket.dev.

title: fix(api): ElevenLabs proxy routes (speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voices) skip enforceApiKeyPolicy
body:
## Summary
Three `/v1/*` routes that proxy to ElevenLabs (`speech-to-text`, `text-to-speech/[voiceId]`, `voices`) never call `enforceApiKeyPolicy`, unlike every sibling billable `/v1/*` route (images, audio, videos, music, ocr, rerank, moderations). Middleware only validates that the presented API key is valid/non-banned/non-expired — budget caps, per-key USD spend limits, custom rate limits, access-schedule windows, and `allowedEndpoints` restrictions are enforced solely by `enforceApiKeyPolicy`, which these three routes skip entirely.

## Evidence
- `src/app/api/v1/speech-to-text/route.ts:10-16`
- `src/app/api/v1/text-to-speech/[voiceId]/route.ts:13-29`
- `src/app/api/v1/voices/route.ts:10-12`
- Shared proxy implementation: `src/app/api/v1/_shared/elevenLabsProxy.ts:46-104`
- Confirmed via grep across every other `/v1/*` media/generation route that `enforceApiKeyPolicy` (`src/shared/utils/apiKeyPolicy.ts`) is called before dispatch in all of them, and is absent from these three.
- The `clientApiPolicy` middleware that does run for all `/v1/*` routes only checks key validity/ban/expiry status — it does not independently enforce budget, rate limits, or endpoint allowlisting; that logic lives exclusively in `enforceApiKeyPolicy`.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/src/app/api/v1/speech-to-text/route.ts#L10-L16

## Why this matters
Any valid API key — including one an operator intentionally scoped to specific endpoints, a tight daily budget, or a restrictive rate limit for a given consumer — can call these three ElevenLabs-backed routes completely unconstrained by those restrictions, consuming the operator's real ElevenLabs quota/spend. This is the same root cause class as issue #12275 ("POST /api/keys silently ignores modelAccessMode/allowedModels/allowedCombos"): a control enforced on one code path but not a structurally identical sibling path.

## Attack or failure scenario
An operator issues an API key to a low-trust consumer, restricting it via `allowedEndpoints`/budget caps to a narrow, cheap set of chat routes. That consumer (or anyone who obtains the key) calls `/v1/text-to-speech/{voiceId}` repeatedly — a route the key was never meant to reach and has no budget ceiling on — running up real ElevenLabs charges against the operator's account with no enforcement stopping it.

## Root cause
`enforceApiKeyPolicy` was added incrementally per-route rather than at a shared middleware/wrapper layer that every `/v1/*` handler passes through by construction, so a new or overlooked route (these three) can silently ship without it.

## Recommended fix
Call `enforceApiKeyPolicy` in `elevenLabsProxy.ts` (the shared implementation all three routes already funnel through) before dispatching to ElevenLabs, matching every sibling `/v1/*` route. Longer-term, consider moving this check into the shared `/v1/*` middleware itself so it cannot be omitted by a future new route.

## Acceptance criteria
- All three ElevenLabs-backed routes reject requests that violate the presented key's budget, rate limit, access-schedule, or `allowedEndpoints` restriction, matching the behavior of sibling `/v1/*` routes.
- A test with a key scoped to exclude these endpoints (or over its budget) receives the same policy-violation response from these routes as from any other `/v1/*` route.

## Suggested labels
bug, api, backend

## Priority
P1

## Severity
Medium-High — real-money abuse vector against the operator's own paid provider account, gated only by possession of any valid key regardless of its intended scope.

## Confidence
Confirmed — verified by reading the shared proxy implementation and confirming the absence of `enforceApiKeyPolicy` via cross-reference against every other `/v1/*` route's call sites.

title: fix(api): hardcoded wildcard CORS in openai-to-gemini-sse.ts bypasses the centralized anonymous-request CORS guard
body:
## Summary
`docs/security/CORS.md` documents that the CORS allowlist is applied exactly once, centrally, in `applyCorsHeaders`/`requestCarriesTokenOrPreflight` (`src/server/cors/origins.ts`), and that this centralized gate specifically withholds a permissive `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` from anonymous requests (no `Authorization`/`x-api-key`/session cookie) on a keyless install — the fail-closed fix for GHSA-7px7-29v2-m97p. The Gemini-compatible response translator hardcodes `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: "*"` unconditionally on every response it returns, on a browser-reachable route, never calling the shared gate at all — bypassing that anonymous-request protection for this specific route.

## Evidence
- `open-sse/translator/response/openai-to-gemini-sse.ts:289,351,359,367,374,429` — six separate response paths each hardcode `"Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*"` directly on the `Response`/headers object.
- `src/app/api/v1beta/models/[...path]/route.ts:4-6,123,126` — this translator is invoked directly from the `/api/v1beta/models/[...path]` route handler (mapped from public path `/v1beta/models/*` via `next.config.mjs:746-751`), which is reachable from a browser.
- `src/server/cors/origins.ts:147-165` (`requestCarriesTokenOrPreflight`) — the documented, intentional design: permissive CORS is safe *only* on token-authed routes (`Authorization`/`x-api-key`/`x-goog-api-key`) or genuinely anonymous+keyless traffic is meant to fall through to fail-closed; cookie-authed routes must stay fail-closed always. This function, and the shared `applyCorsHeaders` it backs, is never called by `openai-to-gemini-sse.ts` — the hardcoded header is what actually reaches the client, unconditionally, regardless of whether the request carries any credential at all.
- This matters concretely because this same audit separately confirms (see the linked "default docker-compose ships `REQUIRE_API_KEY=false`" finding) that a default deployment accepts genuinely anonymous requests — exactly the case the centralized gate exists to protect, and exactly the case this route's hardcoded header bypasses.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/open-sse/translator/response/openai-to-gemini-sse.ts#L289

## Why this matters
On a deployment running with the shipped default (`REQUIRE_API_KEY=false`) and no additional network isolation, a malicious webpage visited by anyone who can reach the OmniRoute instance over the network (LAN, or public internet per the compose-exposure finding) can issue a fetch to this endpoint from the browser and, thanks to the always-present wildcard header, read the streamed LLM completion response back into the page — silently proxying billable LLM usage through the victim's instance and exfiltrating the response content, with no credential and no CORS restriction in the way.

## Attack or failure scenario
Victim runs OmniRoute with defaults, reachable on their LAN (per the compose-exposure finding in this audit). An attacker-controlled webpage the victim's browser loads (or any page on the same network segment probing common local ports) issues a `fetch()` to `http://<victim-host>:<port>/v1beta/models/gemini-...:generateContent` with a crafted body. The route processes it (no API key required under the default config) and returns the response with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, letting the attacker's JavaScript read the completion content directly, bypassing the same-origin policy that would otherwise have blocked a cross-site page from reading the response body.

## Root cause
This translator was written to set its own CORS headers directly rather than going through the project's own centralized, documented CORS gate — an architecture-invariant violation (the docs explicitly call out only one other exception, `src/lib/cloudAgent/api.ts`) that also happens to reintroduce the exact anonymous-request exposure the centralized gate was built to close.

## Recommended fix
Remove the hardcoded `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: "*"` headers from `openai-to-gemini-sse.ts` and route this translator's responses through `applyCorsHeaders`/`requestCarriesTokenOrPreflight` like every other route, so the same fail-closed-for-anonymous-keyless-requests policy applies here too.

## Acceptance criteria
- No response from `/v1beta/models/*` carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or an echoed arbitrary origin) when the request is anonymous and the instance has `REQUIRE_API_KEY=false`.
- A regression test sends an anonymous, credential-less request to this route on a keyless-config instance and asserts the CORS header matches the centralized policy's fail-closed behavior, not a hardcoded wildcard.

## Suggested labels
security (label does not exist on this repo — nearest available: bug), bug, api

## Priority
P1

## Severity
Medium-High — High specifically when combined with the default `REQUIRE_API_KEY=false` deployment (also filed in this audit); the shared CORS module's own documentation confirms this is exactly the scenario it was built to prevent.

## Confidence
Confirmed — read `origins.ts`'s full documented threat model, the route wiring in `next.config.mjs` and the `v1beta` route handler, and confirmed no call to the shared CORS helper exists in `openai-to-gemini-sse.ts`.

title: fix(backend): Adobe Firefly session token and cookie jar written with default file permissions

labels.name: backlog
labels.description: Tracked for future work; not blocking

body:
## Summary
Adobe Firefly (and Notion) browser-login session state — including a live IMS Bearer JWT access token and the full cookie jar (including anti-bot risk tokens) — is written to disk via `writeFileSync`/`mkdirSync` with no `mode` option, leaving the file and its containing directory at the process's default umask permissions (typically `0644`/`0755`, world-readable/traversable). This is inconsistent with this repo's own established, more careful pattern used for the analogous VNC profile directory.

## Evidence
- `open-sse/services/adobeFireflySession.ts:150,235,458` — `writeFileSync(path, JSON.stringify(session, ...), "utf8")` with no `mode`; the session object includes `accessToken` (a live Adobe IMS Bearer JWT) and `cookie` (full Adobe cookie jar, including Forter/Arkose/Sherlock risk-assessment tokens).
- `open-sse/services/adobeFireflyBrowserLogin.ts:413,430` — the directory holding these files is created via `mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true })`, also with no `mode`.
- `open-sse/services/notionThreadSessions.ts:133,136` — the same unhardened write pattern for Notion session state, confirming this is a systemic pattern across browser-login services rather than an isolated oversight.
- Contrast: `src/lib/vncSession/service.ts:131-138` explicitly hardens the analogous profile directory with `mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true, mode: 0o700 })` followed by `chmodSync`, showing the project already has and uses the correct pattern elsewhere.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/open-sse/services/adobeFireflySession.ts#L150

## Why this matters
These files hold live, usable-as-is bearer credentials, not just derived/hashed data — anyone with local read access to the filesystem (another OS user on a shared/multi-tenant host, a process in a container with a shared volume mount, or a background service running under a different, lower-privileged account) can read the file and directly reuse the Adobe/Notion session without needing to compromise OmniRoute's own process.

## Attack or failure scenario
On a multi-user host or a container setup where this data directory is shared via a volume mount with another, less-trusted container/process, that other process reads the world-readable session file and replays the Adobe Firefly bearer token or Notion session cookie directly against the provider's API/site — full account-session takeover without touching OmniRoute at all.

## Root cause
Credential-bearing files were written using the default `writeFileSync`/`mkdirSync` calls without following the restrictive-permissions pattern the codebase already established (and clearly considered necessary) for the structurally identical VNC session-profile case.

## Recommended fix
Apply the same `mode: 0o700` (directories) / `mode: 0o600` (files) pattern used in `src/lib/vncSession/service.ts` to `adobeFireflySession.ts`, `adobeFireflyBrowserLogin.ts`, and `notionThreadSessions.ts` (and audit any other browser-login/session-persistence service for the same gap while this is being fixed, since the pattern has already shown up twice independently).

## Acceptance criteria
- All session/credential files written by browser-login services are created with `0o600` file permissions and `0o700` directory permissions, verified either by an explicit `mode` argument or a `chmodSync` call immediately after creation.
- A shared helper (or lint rule / code-review checklist item) prevents a future browser-login integration from reintroducing the unhardened pattern.

## Suggested labels
security (label does not exist on this repo — nearest available: bug), bug

## Priority
P1

## Severity
High — direct, reusable bearer credentials exposed to any local reader, not a derived or low-value artifact.

## Confidence
Confirmed — verified the exact `writeFileSync`/`mkdirSync` call sites lack a `mode` argument, and confirmed the contrasting hardened pattern exists elsewhere in the same codebase.

title: fix(docker): VNC browser CDP bridge is unauthenticated and reachable from co-located containers

labels.name: docker
labels.description: Pull requests that update docker code

labels.name: backlog
labels.description: Tracked for future work; not blocking

body:
## Summary
The VNC browser-login container proxies Chrome's DevTools Protocol (CDP), which normally binds to `127.0.0.1:9222` inside the container, out to `0.0.0.0:9223` with no authentication, IP allowlist, or origin check. CDP has no built-in auth of its own — anyone who can reach port 9223 gets full remote control of the browser (arbitrary JavaScript execution in-page, cookie/localStorage theft, navigation) during what is meant to be a private, credential-bearing provider login session.

## Evidence
- `docker/vnc-browser/chromium/cdp-bridge.py:11-12,44-51` — raw TCP proxy from the loopback-bound Chrome CDP port to `0.0.0.0:9223`, no auth/token/origin check anywhere in the bridge.
- `docker/vnc-browser/chromium/Dockerfile:19-24` — `EXPOSE 3000 9222 9223`.
- `src/lib/vncSession/service.ts:213-216` mitigates *host*-external exposure by publishing the container's ports via `-p 127.0.0.1::PORT`, but this only protects against connections from outside the Docker host — any other container sharing the same Docker network (the default bridge network, sibling containers, or Docker Desktop's shared VM networking) can reach `0.0.0.0:9223` directly by the container's internal IP, bypassing that restriction entirely.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/docker/vnc-browser/chromium/cdp-bridge.py#L44-L51

## Why this matters
This container exists specifically to let users log into LLM-provider web accounts (e.g. via browser automation) so OmniRoute can capture session cookies/tokens for API use. An unauthenticated CDP endpoint reachable from anywhere on the same Docker network gives full control of that browser session during exactly the window when it holds live, high-value credentials — an attacker doesn't need to steal the session file from disk (see the related plaintext-credential-file finding filed alongside this one); they can drive the browser directly while it's authenticated.

## Attack or failure scenario
Any other container on the same Docker network (a sibling service in the same compose stack, or an unrelated container if the host runs multiple Docker Compose projects on the default bridge network) connects to the VNC browser container's internal IP on port 9223 and issues raw CDP commands — e.g. `Runtime.evaluate` to read `document.cookie`, or `Network.getAllCookies` — exfiltrating the live provider session without ever touching the host-published port.

## Root cause
CDP was designed to be used only over a trusted, isolated channel (loopback, or a channel with its own auth layer in front). The bridge in this repo turns loopback-only access into network-reachable access without adding any of the auth/allowlisting that step requires.

## Recommended fix
Add an authentication layer to `cdp-bridge.py` (e.g. a shared-secret token required in the connection handshake, checked before proxying any bytes) or, more simply, do not proxy CDP off loopback within the container network at all — keep the bridge's listen address on `127.0.0.1` and reach it only via `docker exec`/`nsenter` from the OmniRoute controller process rather than over the Docker network, or use Docker network isolation (a dedicated internal network with no other containers attached) as defense-in-depth alongside a token check.

## Acceptance criteria
- Port 9223 (or wherever CDP is proxied) is not reachable by an unauthenticated peer container without presenting a valid credential/token.
- A test or documented manual check confirms a connection from another container on the same bridge network is rejected without the token.

## Suggested labels
security (label does not exist on this repo — nearest available: bug), bug, docker

## Priority
P1

## Severity
High — full session/browser takeover from any co-located container, no credentials required.

## Confidence
Confirmed — read the bridge script's bind address and the Dockerfile's exposed ports directly; no auth check present in the proxy code.

title: docs(docker): document the host-root trust boundary of the docker.sock mount in the cli profile

labels.name: docker
labels.description: Pull requests that update docker code

labels.name: backlog
labels.description: Tracked for future work; not blocking

body:
## Summary
The `omniroute-cli` Docker Compose service (profile `cli`) bind-mounts the host's Docker socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`) into a container that also globally installs four unpinned (`latest`) AI coding-agent CLIs capable of executing arbitrary shell/tool commands, plus a read-write mount of the host repository. This combination is undocumented anywhere in the README or `docs/` tree and gives any command executed by one of those agents an effective path to root on the host via the Docker socket.

## Evidence
- `docker-compose.yml:158-177` (service `omniroute-cli`, profile `cli`):
  - `/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock` (line ~173) — no comment explaining the risk, unlike the Redis bind-address comment nine lines above the equivalent section for that service.
  - `${AUTO_UPDATE_HOST_REPO_DIR:-.}:/workspace/omniroute:rw` (line ~175) — read-write host repo mount in the same container.
- `Dockerfile:348` (target `runner-cli`, the build target this service uses): `npm install -g --no-audit --no-fund @openai/codex @anthropic-ai/claude-code droid openclaw@latest` — four agent CLIs installed with no version pins.
- `grep -rn "docker.sock" README.md docs/` returns no results — this mount is not documented or flagged as a power-user/security tradeoff anywhere a user would see before enabling the `cli` profile.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/docker-compose.yml#L158-L177

## Why this matters
Docker socket access is equivalent to root on the host — any process that can talk to `/var/run/docker.sock` can start a privileged, host-network, host-filesystem-mounted container and fully escape. Placing that socket inside the same container as multiple general-purpose AI agent CLIs (whose entire purpose is executing commands on request, including from remote/untrusted instructions such as prompt-injected content in a fetched web page or file) turns any agent misbehavior or prompt injection into a full host compromise, not just a contained sandbox escape.

## Attack or failure scenario
An operator enables the `cli` profile so an AI agent can help manage their OmniRoute deployment. The agent is later given (directly or via prompt injection in content it reads, e.g. a webpage, email, or file it's asked to summarize) a command that creates a new Docker container with `-v /:/host --privileged`, mounting the entire host filesystem read-write into a new container the agent controls — a standard Docker-socket container-escape technique. Because none of the agent CLIs are pinned, a compromised or backdoored release of any of the four packages would have the same access without requiring any prompt injection at all.

## Root cause
No isolation between "give an AI agent shell access to help operate this service" and "give that same environment root-equivalent host access via the Docker socket." The mount was added without a corresponding trust-boundary comment or opt-in confirmation, unlike the project's own pattern for lower-stakes decisions (e.g. the Redis bind-address comment).

## Recommended fix
- Remove the Docker socket mount from `omniroute-cli` unless a specific, narrow feature requires it; if a feature does require Docker control, use a scoped Docker socket proxy (e.g. a `docker-socket-proxy` sidecar with an explicit allowlisted API subset) instead of the raw socket.
- If the raw socket must stay for now, add an explicit, prominent warning in the compose file (matching the Redis precedent) and in the README/docs section describing the `cli` profile, stating plainly that enabling it grants host-root-equivalent access to anything the contained agents execute.
- Pin the four agent CLI packages to specific versions in the Dockerfile and update them deliberately, rather than tracking `latest`.

## Acceptance criteria
- The `cli` profile either no longer mounts the raw Docker socket, or its documentation (compose comment + README/docs) explicitly states the host-root-equivalent risk before an operator opts in.
- Agent CLI versions in the `runner-cli` Dockerfile stage are pinned.

## Suggested labels
security (label does not exist on this repo — nearest available: bug), bug, docker

## Priority
P1

## Severity
High — requires the operator to have opted into the `cli` profile, but the risk is undocumented and the blast radius (host root) is severe.

## Confidence
Confirmed — verified the exact compose lines, the Dockerfile install command, and the absence of any documentation via direct grep across README.md and docs/.

title: fix(backend): webhook outbound URL guard is hostname-string-only (DNS-rebinding SSRF)
body:
## Summary
The outbound-URL guard that protects webhook delivery (`isPrivateHost`, `isCloudMetadataHost`, `parseAndValidateWebhookUrl`) validates only the literal hostname string in the configured URL — it never resolves DNS before deciding whether a target is private/metadata/public. An attacker-controlled domain whose DNS record points at `169.254.169.254` (cloud instance metadata) or an RFC1918 address passes every string-based check, and the real `fetch()` call that follows resolves DNS itself and connects to the actual internal target. The same string-only check also gates whether the webhook-test endpoint redacts the response body, so the full internal response is returned to the caller.

## Evidence
- `src/shared/network/privateHost.ts:58-103` (`isPrivateHost`) — classifies by regex/set membership against the literal hostname, no DNS resolution.
- `src/shared/network/outboundUrlGuard.ts:74-82` (`isCloudMetadataHost`) — same pattern for metadata hostnames/IPs.
- `src/shared/network/outboundUrlGuardPolicy.ts:111-133` (`parseAndValidateWebhookUrl`) — the composed guard used by the webhook path; no DNS-resolve-then-pin-to-IP step.
- `src/app/api/webhooks/[id]/test/route.ts:34-38` — decides whether to redact the response body using the same string-only `isPrivateHost(parsed.hostname)` check, so a hostname that resolves to an internal address at request time still gets its full (up to 2048-byte) response body returned in the JSON response.
- `src/lib/webhookDispatcher.ts:45,78` — the real delivery path (`dispatchEvent`), fires automatically on app events for any already-configured webhook, not just the manual test endpoint.
- The identical bug class was already fixed for a different feature: `src/shared/network/remoteImageFetch.ts:67-97` explicitly resolves DNS and pins the outbound request to the validated IP, citing GHSA-cmhj-wh2f-9cgx. That fix was never applied to the webhook path.
- Confirmed by a second independent read: the open-sse executors that accept a tenant-supplied custom provider `baseUrl` (`open-sse/executors/base.ts:424-430,654,929`, `glm.ts:468`, `nlpcloud.ts:474`, `oneminai.ts:243`, all tagged `// GHSA-4f49`) correctly reuse this same shared guard — meaning the DNS-rebinding weakness is inherited by every custom-baseURL provider dispatch as well, not just webhooks.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/src/shared/network/outboundUrlGuardPolicy.ts#L111-L133

## Why this matters
This is a classic SSRF-via-DNS-rebinding gap on a feature whose entire purpose is validated outbound HTTP to operator-supplied URLs. On any cloud deployment with an attached IMDS role, this is a path to credential theft from the metadata service. Even off-cloud, it reaches internal-network services (databases, internal admin panels, other containers on the same Docker network) that the private-IP check was specifically meant to block, and leaks their response bodies back to the attacker via the test endpoint.

## Attack or failure scenario
An attacker with access to create/test a webhook (requires `requireManagementAuth`, so this is post-authentication — but note finding "Default docker-compose ships unauthenticated" in this same audit means that bar may be zero in a default deployment) registers a webhook URL on a domain they control, e.g. `evil.example.com`, whose DNS A record they set to `169.254.169.254`. `parseAndValidateWebhookUrl` sees the hostname string `evil.example.com`, which matches no private/metadata pattern, and passes. The subsequent real `fetch()` resolves `evil.example.com` to `169.254.169.254` and requests cloud instance credentials, returning them in the (unredacted, because the redaction check uses the same broken hostname classification) response body via the test endpoint.

## Root cause
Validating a URL's destination by inspecting the literal hostname string is fundamentally insufficient against DNS rebinding — the check and the actual network connection happen at different times against different resolutions, and nothing pins them together. The codebase already has the correct pattern (`remoteImageFetch.ts`) but it was not applied uniformly to every outbound-fetch call site.

## Recommended fix
Apply the same DNS-resolve-then-pin-to-validated-IP pattern already used in `remoteImageFetch.ts` (GHSA-cmhj-wh2f-9cgx fix) to `outboundUrlGuardPolicy.ts` / `outboundUrlGuard.ts`, and route both the webhook test endpoint and `webhookDispatcher.ts` through the corrected guard. Since `open-sse/executors/base.ts` and the other GHSA-4f49-tagged executors share the same guard module, fixing it in one place closes the gap for both webhooks and custom-provider-baseURL dispatch.

## Acceptance criteria
- A webhook (or custom provider baseURL) pointed at a domain that resolves to `169.254.169.254` or any RFC1918 address is rejected at request time, not just by hostname-string inspection.
- The webhook test endpoint's redaction decision uses the same resolved-IP classification as the connection itself, so a successful bypass cannot also leak the response body.
- A regression test exercises a mocked DNS resolution pointing a "public-looking" hostname at a private/metadata IP and confirms the request is blocked.

## Suggested labels
security (label does not exist on this repo — nearest available: bug), bug, backend

## Priority
P0

## Severity
High (Critical on any cloud deployment with an IMDS role attached to the instance).

## Confidence
Confirmed — read all three guard functions in full and the two call sites; no DNS resolution step exists anywhere in this path before the real `fetch()`.

title: fix(docker): compose defaults bind 0.0.0.0 while REQUIRE_API_KEY=false leaves /v1 anonymous

labels.name: docker
labels.description: Pull requests that update docker code

body:
## Summary
The shipped `docker-compose.yml` / `docker-compose.prod.yml` publish the dashboard, API, and live-WS ports with no host-IP scoping (binds `0.0.0.0`), and `.env.example` ships `REQUIRE_API_KEY=false`. A default `docker compose --profile base up -d` (or the `cli`/prod variants) with no `.env` edits exposes an unauthenticated LLM proxy and dashboard to every network interface on the host, including any LAN or, on a cloud VM, the public internet.

## Evidence
- `.env.example:373` — `REQUIRE_API_KEY=false`
- `docker-compose.yml:40-42,129-131,198-201` — `API_HOST`/`LIVE_WS_HOST`/`HOSTNAME` default to `0.0.0.0`; port mappings (e.g. `"${DASHBOARD_PORT:-20128}:${DASHBOARD_PORT:-20128}"`) carry no host-IP prefix, so Docker publishes on `0.0.0.0` by default.
- `docker-compose.prod.yml:66-69` — same pattern in the production compose file.
- Contrast: the `redis` service in the same `docker-compose.yml` binds `${REDIS_BIND_HOST:-127.0.0.1}:...` with an explanatory comment about the exact risk this issue describes — the app's own ports were never given the same treatment.
- Source-level default is safe in isolation (`src/server/ws/liveServer.ts:53`, `src/lib/apiBridgeServer.ts:186` both default to loopback), but the compose files override it via env defaults, and there is no code-level refusal to bind non-loopback without `REQUIRE_API_KEY=true`.
- Related prior fixes that did not close this gap: #7722 (fixed only the `README.md` `docker run` example to use `-p 127.0.0.1:...`), #2034 (accepted request to respect `HOST`/`HOSTNAME` instead of hardcoding `0.0.0.0`, not yet implemented).

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/docker-compose.yml#L40-L42

## Why this matters
This is the default, documented path to running OmniRoute via Docker. An operator who follows the README's quickest path — clone, copy `.env.example` to `.env`, `docker compose up` — gets an unauthenticated proxy that can execute billable calls against every configured LLM provider, read/export stored provider credentials via any admin route, and (per the sibling MITM/browser-automation and webhook findings filed alongside this one) reach further internal functionality, all without a network firewall being anything but the last line of defense.

## Attack or failure scenario
An operator deploys with defaults on a cloud VM or a home LAN without additional firewalling. Anyone who can reach the host on the dashboard/API port (a LAN neighbor, a cloud security-group misconfiguration, a container escape from an unrelated workload on the same Docker bridge network) gets full unauthenticated access to the proxy and dashboard — no credentials required.

## Root cause
Two independent defaults compound: (1) the compose files bind every OmniRoute-owned service to all interfaces instead of loopback-by-default, breaking the same-file precedent already set for Redis; (2) `REQUIRE_API_KEY=false` is the example/default value rather than requiring an explicit opt-out. Neither the app nor the compose file enforces "if bound non-loopback, an API key or auth mechanism must be configured."

## Recommended fix
- Change the compose port mappings to bind `127.0.0.1` by default (matching the Redis pattern), with a documented `API_HOST=0.0.0.0` opt-in for operators who intentionally want LAN/WAN exposure.
- Either flip `REQUIRE_API_KEY` to default `true`, or add a startup check that refuses to bind a non-loopback interface unless `REQUIRE_API_KEY=true` (or an equivalent auth mechanism) is explicitly set, logging a clear error instead of silently starting unauthenticated.
- Implement the accepted #2034 request to respect `HOST`/`HOSTNAME` instead of hardcoding `0.0.0.0` inside the compose defaults.

## Acceptance criteria
- `docker compose up` with a freshly copied `.env` (no manual edits) does not expose any OmniRoute port on a non-loopback interface unless the operator explicitly set `API_HOST`/`LIVE_WS_HOST` to a non-loopback value.
- Binding to a non-loopback interface with `REQUIRE_API_KEY=false` either fails fast with a clear error, or is impossible without an explicit override flag.
- `docker-compose.prod.yml` matches the same policy.

## Suggested labels
security (label does not exist on this repo — nearest available: bug, docker), bug, docker, production-readiness (label does not exist on this repo)

## Priority
P0

## Severity
Critical — this is the default, documented deployment path, not an edge case, and combines with other findings in this audit (webhook SSRF, admin/export routes) into full unauthenticated remote functionality.

## Confidence
Confirmed — read the exact compose files, `.env.example`, and the two related prior issues (#7722, #2034) confirming this gap is known but still open.

title: fix(cli): detect npm-global Claude .cmd shims under Program Files on Windows
body:
## Summary

Fixes #12563.

Maintainer correction: npm-prefix candidates were already derived from `npm config get prefix`. The real hole was permanently caching a failed prefix as `""` (deleting every npm-derived candidate for the process lifetime), plus thin Windows PATH enrichment vs macOS login-shell enrichment. `settings_found_binary_unresolved` is the settings-fallback symptom of that lookup miss — not its own bug.

This PR:
- Soft-fails npm prefix detection (retry window + live `npm_config_prefix` recovery; no permanent empty cache)
- Enriches Windows lookup PATH with npm-prefix / `%APPDATA%\npm` / nvm / `%ProgramFiles%\nodejs`
- Keeps the stock Node MSI `%ProgramFiles%\nodejs\*.cmd` safety net
- Extracts helpers so `cliRuntime.ts` stays under its frozen file-size cap

Different hole than #7831 / #7774 (`.ps1` / known-path short-circuit).

## What changed

- `cliRuntimeNpmPrefix.ts`: soft-fail / retry prefix cache
- `cliRuntimeWindowsNode.ts`: Program Files safety net + broader Windows PATH merge
- Unit tests for prefix soft-fail and custom-prefix PATH enrichment

## Test plan

- [x] `tests/unit/cli-runtime-windows-node-12563.test.ts` (6/6)
- [x] `tests/unit/cli-runtime-npm-prefix-12563.test.ts` (3/3)
- [ ] `tests/unit/cli-runtime-npm-cmd-shim-12563.test.ts` (win32 tsx runner)
- [ ] Dashboard Claude CLI shows runnable with a Program Files npm shim
- [ ] Custom npm prefix / nvm-windows still resolves when Electron PATH omits it

title: fix(i18n/build/ci): ICU-escape 381 message values, externalize tiktoken, add blocking UI-ICU gate
body: ## Summary Three tightly-related fixes, verified live on the latest `release/v3.8.51`: 1. **`fix(i18n)`** — ICU-escape **381 message values** containing raw `` / literal `{...}` across all **42 locale catalogs** (`src/i18n/messages/*.json`). 2. **`fix(build)`** — externalize `tiktoken` in `next.config.mjs` so `tiktoken_bg.wasm` resolves at runtime. 3. **`chore(ci)`** — add a **blocking** `check:ui-icu` gate that compiles every message value with `IntlMessageFormat` (next-intl's parser), so this defect class can never ship again. ## Background A message value containing a raw `` or literal `{...}` fails to compile under `IntlMessageFormat`. At runtime the component silently breaks — the RSC/Flight path throws `INVALID_MESSAGE` and the UI falls back to showing the raw i18n key. This exact class shipped repeatedly: - **#12302** — `ccOnboardingKeyPlaceholder` = `` (crashed the Claude Code onboarding block) - **#12505** — `OMNIROUTE_AUTO_SYNC_CLAUDE_PROFILES.description` = `~/.claude/profiles//settings.json` (Feature Flags page showed the raw key) - **#12559** — `featureFlagExposeFunctionalGatewayMirrorsDescription` = raw `/` - plus literal JSON/regex paste-hint examples (`[{ json, name?, email? }...]`), a service-account JSON placeholder, regex samples, a broken ``/`{` characters must render. HTML entities would corrupt the pasted content. Every single change was asserted **render-identical** (`new IntlMessageFormat(fixed).format() === original`) by `scripts/ad-hoc/fix-invalid-icu.mjs`; the only deliberate wording change is the `nl` `bold"`) and normal ICU (`{count, plural, ...}`) compile fine — no false positives, pinned by `tests/unit/i18n-ui-icu.test.ts` (10 tests). Wired into the blocking `i18n-ui-coverage` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. ## The tiktoken fix (commit 2) `tiktoken` resolves `tiktoken_bg.wasm` at runtime via `fs.readFileSync` relative to `__dirname`; bundled by Turbopack that lookup fails ("Missing tiktoken_bg.wasm") and 500s every route touching codex-chatgpt-web token estimation (e.g. `GET /api/providers`). Externalizing it (like `sqlite-vec` / `better-sqlite3`) keeps the require at runtime. ## Verification - `check:ui-icu` → **PASS — all 545,817 messages in 42 catalogs compile** - `tests/unit/i18n-ui-icu.test.ts` → **10/10 pass** - `check-ui-value-drift` (against base) → **PASS** - `check-ui-keys-coverage` → **PASS** Note: `intl-messageformat` is currently a transitive dep of `next-intl` (^11.1.0) — the gate requires it, so if that dependency is ever dropped it should be promoted to a direct dependency.

title: fix(sse): prefer cgroup PSI for chat admission
body:
## Summary

Chat admission's resource-pressure sampler read host-wide `/proc/pressure/memory`. In Docker that file is the **machine**, not the container: a swapping host 503s idle OmniRoute with `resource_pressure` even when the cgroup is well under its limit (V8/cgroup ratios stay `normal`).

Prefer this unit's cgroup v2 `memory.pressure` when it parses. Keep `/proc/pressure/memory` only as fallback (bare metal, cgroup v1, missing file).

## Test plan

- [x] `node --import tsx/esm --test tests/unit/resource-pressure-sampler.test.ts`
  - prefers cgroup PSI when both files exist and disagree
  - falls back to `/proc/pressure/memory` when the cgroup pressure file is absent
  - existing sampler cases still pass
- [ ] Docker host under memory PSI, container idle: `/v1/chat/completions` is not 503 `resource_pressure`

title: fix: backfill missing usage.kiloPass* translations in 39 locales (+ pt-only flag description)
body:
The Kilo Pass / Kilo Code balance UI (#12178, added 2026-09-01) introduced 7 new strings under `usage.*` in `en.json`, but only **de, pt-BR, vi** have them translated — the other **39 locales** (`ar, az, bg, bn, cs, da, es, fa, fi, fr, gu, he, hi, hu, id, in, it, ja, ko, mr, ms, nl, no, phi, pl, pt, ro, ru, sk, sv, sw, ta, te, th, tr, uk-UA, ur, zh-CN, zh-TW`) are missing all 7 keys and fall back to English (or show raw keys) on the Kilo Pass usage meter.

## Missing keys (en values)
| Key | en value |
|---|---|
| `usage.kiloAccountBalance` | "Account Balance" |
| `usage.kiloPassBonus` | "Available bonus" |
| `usage.kiloPassMeterLabel` | "Kilo Pass usage meter" |
| `usage.kiloPassPaid` | "Paid" |
| `usage.kiloPassRemaining` | "Remaining" |
| `usage.kiloPassRenews` | "Renews {count} days" |
| `usage.kiloPassUsageLabel` | "This month's usage" |

## Also
- `featureFlagOmnirouteDisableThinkingLevelVariantsDescription` is missing **only from `pt.json`** (all other 41 locales have it; `pt-BR` has it).

## How this was found
A full missing/empty/placeholder sweep of all 43 catalogs vs `en.json` (12,951 keys): **274 missing-key occurrences = 8 distinct keys** (the 7 above × 39 locales + the 1 `pt` flag description). Zero empty/null values anywhere. The 1,613 `__MISSING__:` placeholders across 47 other keys are the intentional value-drift escape hatch, not defects.

`de`/`pt-BR`/`vi` are already complete and can serve as reference for the backfill. The existing `check-ui-keys-coverage` gate counts key *presence*, so it won't flag this class until a key is actually deleted — a per-key missing-list would help here, but the immediate ask is just the backfill.

title: feat: add strict ICU compile gate for all UI locale catalogs (check:ui-icu)
body: Companion to #12302 / #12505 / #12559. A sweep of every message in every locale catalog with `IntlMessageFormat` (the exact parser next-intl uses) found **302 messages across 43 locales that fail to compile** — the same defect class that has now broken pages 4 times (Claude Code onboarding, Feature Flags page ×2, Kilo Pass labels). next-intl silently swallows these failures at runtime (`createTranslator` does not surface them), so every one of these pages was quietly falling back to raw key names. ## Proposal: a blocking CI gate that compiles all 556,619 messages `scripts/i18n/check-ui-icu.mjs` (168 lines): - Compiles **every message value** in `src/i18n/messages/*.json` (43 catalogs, 556,619 messages, ~6s) with `IntlMessageFormat`. - Any compile error (`INVALID_TAG`, `UNCLOSED_TAG`, `MALFORMED_ARGUMENT`, …) exits 1 → PR fails. - `--warn` / `--json` flags, exported pure helpers (`findInvalidMessages`, `flattenLeaves`), matching the conventions of `check-ui-value-drift.mjs`. - Unit-tested: `tests/unit/i18n-ui-icu.test.ts` (10 cases — both known bug classes throw, legit `t.rich` rich-text compiles, escaped values pass, no false positives). - Wired into the blocking `i18n-ui-coverage` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` via `npm run check:ui-icu` (added to `package.json`). Legitimate rich-text (`"bold"` used with `t.rich`) and normal ICU (`{count, plural, ...}`) compile fine — no false positives. ## The 302 failures it would have caught (all fixed locally, render-identical) `scripts/ad-hoc/fix-invalid-icu.mjs` applied per-key transforms and **asserted `format(fixed) === original` for every single change** — every fix is provably render-identical. Breakdown: 1. **Raw `` in plain-`t()` messages** (live bugs, same class as the filed issues): - `featureFlagExposeFunctionalGatewayMirrorsDescription` = `Advertise / mirror ids...` — 43 locales (filed as #12559) - `ccOnboardingKeyPlaceholder` = `` — 43 locales (filed as #12302) - `OMNIROUTE_AUTO_SYNC_CLAUDE_PROFILES.description` = `~/.claude/profiles//settings.json` — 43 locales (filed as #12505) 2. **Literal JSON/regex paste-hint examples** with raw `{...}` braces (e.g. `[{ json, name?, email? }...]` schema hints) that render as raw text but fail strict ICU parsing — wrapped the literal braces in ICU quotes (render-identical). 3. **`{" "}` artifacts** in `phi`/`sv` status labels (`pinned`/`lastUsed`) — quoted fragment. 4. **Broken rich-text tag** in Dutch (`deze`) — corrected to a matching tag. Result: **all 556,619 messages in all 43 catalogs now compile cleanly.** ## Verified - `npm run check:ui-icu` → PASS (0 failures) - `check-ui-value-drift` (existing blocking gate) → PASS — the 2 locales whose English changed (`vi`, `pt-BR`) were refreshed to track it - `check-ui-keys-coverage` → PASS - `tests/unit/i18n-ui-icu.test.ts` → 10/10 - Locale diff is surgical (390/390 lines across 43 files, no reformat noise) ## Notes - `intl-messageformat` is currently a **transitive** dep of `next-intl` (^11.1.0) — the gate requires it; if upstream ever drops that dependency, promote it to a direct dependency. - Suggested follow-up: apply the same strict compile check to the CLI i18n catalogs (`scripts/check/check-cli-i18n.mjs` covers keys but not ICU validity).

title: fix: escape raw <gateway-alias>/<model> tags in functional-gateway-mirrors flag description across all locale catalogs
body:
Same defect class as #12302 and #12505: a message value with a raw `<tag>` that is rendered through plain `t()` (not `t.rich`) fails ICU compilation under next-intl and silently breaks the page — the card falls back to showing the raw key name instead of the description.

## Environment
- Branch: `release/v3.8.51` @ `073b98462` (latest, fully synced)
- Reported from a fork; Windows 11, Node 24, dev mode

## Symptom
The `OMNIROUTE_EXPOSE_FUNCTIONAL_GATEWAY_MIRRORS` flag card on `/dashboard/settings/feature-flags` renders the raw key name instead of the description, and the browser console logs `INVALID_MESSAGE: INVALID_TAG`.

## Root cause
All 43 locale catalogs (`src/i18n/messages/*.json`) contain:

```json
"featureFlagExposeFunctionalGatewayMirrorsDescription": "Advertise <gateway-alias>/<model> mirror ids on /v1/models ..."
```

The Feature Flags grid renders flag descriptions via **plain `t()`**:

- `src/app/(dashboard)/dashboard/settings/components/FeatureFlagsGrid.tsx:140`
  `matchesSearch(t(`definitions.${f.key}.description`), debouncedSearch)`

next-intl parses `<gateway-alias>` and `<model>` as unknown rich-text tags with no matching element → the message fails to compile → `t()` falls back to the key name.

`featureFlagDefinitions.ts:540` wires the key (`descriptionI18nKey`).

## Verified fix (already applied locally, all 43 files)
Wrap the literal tags in **ICU single quotes** — renders identical text but compiles:

```
"description": "Advertise '<gateway-alias>'/'<model>' mirror ids on /v1/models ..."
```

Verified two ways:
1. `IntlMessageFormat` (next-intl's parser): `Advertise '<gateway-alias>'/'<model>' mirror ids...` → renders exactly `Advertise <gateway-alias>/<model> mirror ids...` with no error.
2. Live page: the flag card now shows the full description; console clean.

## Why not `<`/`>`
The value is a human-readable explanation of mirror-id syntax — the literal angle brackets must render (`<gateway-alias>/<model>` is an id pattern users see). HTML entities would display incorrectly.

## Notes
- This was the 4th live instance of this bug class: #12302 (`ccOnboardingKeyPlaceholder`), #12505 (`OMNIROUTE_AUTO_SYNC_CLAUDE_PROFILES.description`), and the `{" "}` artifacts in `phi`/`sv`. A strict ICU compile gate for all catalogs (`npm run check:ui-icu`, wired into CI) now exists to prevent regressions — see the companion issue.

title: docs(reference): sync FEATURE_FLAGS.md with featureFlagDefinitions
body:
## Summary

- `docs/reference/FEATURE_FLAGS.md:10-13` promises that its catalog is "generated to match [`featureFlagDefinitions.ts`] 1:1", but on `release/v3.8.51` it had drifted: 20 of the 54 keys in `FEATURE_FLAG_DEFINITIONS` (`src/shared/constants/featureFlagDefinitions.ts:14-655`) had no row (3 security, 2 network, 2 policies, 11 runtime, 2 cli), two rows were not flags at all (`INPUT_SANITIZER_BLOCK_THRESHOLD` and its legacy alias `INJECTION_GUARD_BLOCK_THRESHOLD` are plain env vars read in `src/shared/utils/injectionSeverity.ts:48-49`, with no DB override or dashboard toggle), the summary line said 37 flags and the `GET` example said "all 33 flags" / `"total": 33`, the per-category headings were stale (7/8/3/11/3/3 vs 10/9/5/22/5/3), and the `OMNIROUTE_ENABLE_LIVE_WS` row named port 20129 while the code default is 20132 (`src/app/api/v1/ws/route.ts:30`, `src/server/ws/liveServer.ts:4`).
- The six catalog tables are regenerated from the definitions (category, type, default, `requiresRestart`), in definition order. Rows that already existed keep their curated wording; the 20 new rows use the definition's `description` (plus the `Values:` list for the two enums). The two threshold env vars move to a note under the tables that points at `ENVIRONMENT.md`, where they are already documented. Counts, the JSON example, and the frontmatter are refreshed. No values of previously documented rows changed (the static check found zero type/default mismatches on the base).
- Guard: `tests/unit/feature-flags-doc-sync-static.test.ts` parses the catalog and asserts, against `FEATURE_FLAG_DEFINITIONS`, that every defined flag has a row, every row is a defined flag, category/type/default/restart match, and the heading counts and the "N flags across M categories" total match. Red on the base (3 of 4 fail), green here.
- `scripts/check/check-fabricated-docs.mjs` (strict in `quality.yml`) would have failed on six of the new rows with "env var is never read", because `resolveFeatureFlag()` reads `process.env[definition.key]` dynamically (`src/shared/utils/featureFlags.ts:45`) and the literal scan cannot see it. The checker now reads every `key:` in `featureFlagDefinitions.ts` into its documented-env-var index; this generalizes the existing one-off `MODELS_CATALOG_PREFIX_MODE` allowlist entry, which is removed. Its own suite (`tests/unit/check-fabricated-docs.test.ts`, 25/25) and the strict run stay green. No production code changes.

## Related Issues

- No open issue tracks this drift (`gh issue list --search "FEATURE_FLAGS"` returns nothing relevant).
- Related to #12486, which adds `REASONING_REPLAY_ENABLED` to `featureFlagDefinitions.ts`; once it lands the new static test will ask for its row (one line in the Runtime table).

## Validation

- [x] Change type: other (documentation + doc-accuracy checker + static test)
- [x] Focused tests and category gates from the golden path: `tests/unit/feature-flags-doc-sync-static.test.ts` 4/4, `tests/unit/check-fabricated-docs.test.ts` 25/25, `npm run check:fabricated-docs` (strict) OK, `npm run check:docs-sync` PASS, `npm run check:docs-counts` OK, `node scripts/check/check-doc-links.mjs` PASS (955 links), `npm run check:changelog-integrity` OK
- [ ] `npm run lint` — not run repository-wide; `eslint` and `prettier --check` on the touched files exit 0 (`scripts/check/*.mjs` is eslint-ignored by the repo config; prettier applied)
- [x] Reconciled with the current active release base `release/v3.8.51`; focused checks rerun afterward
- [x] Production-code changes include a new or updated automated test in this PR (no `src/` change; the doc gets a static test)
- SonarQube is temporarily opt-in while the private project has no quota; it is not a PR gate.

## Tests Added Or Updated

- `tests/unit/feature-flags-doc-sync-static.test.ts` (new, 4 cases): defined flags all present; no undefined rows; category/type/default/restart parity; heading and total counts. On the base doc: `not ok 1`, `not ok 2`, `ok 3`, `not ok 4`. With this change: 4/4.
- No production code changed. `tests/unit/check-fabricated-docs.test.ts` is unchanged and green; its case "real documentation has no fabricated claims" is the one that would have caught the six dynamically resolved flags without the checker change.

## Coverage Notes

- No `src/`, `open-sse/`, `electron/`, or `bin/` files changed. The checker change is exercised by `tests/unit/check-fabricated-docs.test.ts` (which calls `buildCodebaseIndex` on the real repo) and by the strict run.

## Reviewer Notes

- Descriptions for the 20 new rows are taken verbatim from `featureFlagDefinitions.ts`; the test deliberately does not compare descriptions, so the doc can keep curated wording (cross-links, `**Danger.**`) without churn.
- `OMNIROUTE_ENABLE_LIVE_WS`: only the port number in the description changed (20129 -> 20132). If 20129 is meant somewhere, it is not the default in `src/app/api/v1/ws/route.ts`.

title: fix(i18n): translate the home Recent Requests panel and topology legend
body:
## Summary

- On a non-English dashboard the home page mixed languages in the two live widgets. The "Recent Requests" panel (`src/app/(dashboard)/home/HomeRecentRequests.tsx`) already reads every label through `useTranslations("home")`, but the five keys it uses (`home.recentRequests`, `recentRequestsEmpty`, `recentRequestsModel`, `recentRequestsTokens`, `recentRequestsWhen`) shipped in #10900 as verbatim English copies in 39 of the 41 non-English catalogs (only pt-BR and vi were translated). A verbatim copy is invisible to every i18n gate: `check-ui-keys-coverage` counts it as covered, `sync-ui-keys` only backfills absent keys, and `check-ui-value-drift` only sees English values that change. So the panel rendered "RECENT REQUESTS / Model / In / Out / When" in es, fr, de, it, ja and every other locale.
- The Provider Topology legend (`src/app/(dashboard)/dashboard/HomeProviderTopologySection.tsx`) borrowed three labels from unrelated namespaces: `common.active`, `settings.recent` (the memory-retrieval "Chronological window" toggle, itself an English copy in 33 locales) and `analytics.modelStatusError` (lower-case "error" in es). The result in Spanish was "Activo · Recent · error" under a Spanish title.
- Fix: the legend now owns its three labels, `home.topologyLegendActive` / `topologyLegendRecent` / `topologyLegendError`, next to the `home.activeError` subtitle they sit under, with consistent capitalisation per locale. The recent-requests keys get real translations in es, pt, fr, de and it (pt-BR and vi were already correct); the legend keys are translated in es, pt, pt-BR, fr, de, it and vi. Every other locale gets the repo's `__MISSING__:<english>` marker (the form #12401 used for new keys) instead of a silent English copy — the runtime still falls back to English there, but the keys are now visible to `i18n:sync-ui --translate-markers`. Where a locale already had a translated `common.active` / `settings.recent` / `analytics.modelStatusError`, that translation is reused for the legend rather than a marker (54 reused, 48 markers across the 34 locales I did not translate by hand). No English value changed, so the value-drift gate is unaffected.
- Deliberately out of scope (same root cause, different surface, kept for a follow-up so this PR stays one defect): the `FirstRunReadinessCard` `home.readiness*` keys (10) plus `home.stepError`, `home.requestsShort`, `home.aliasLabel` are also English copies in es and most locales; `analytics.modelStatusError` is still lower-case "error" in es on the analytics page; `settings.recent` remains an English copy in 33 locales on the memory settings tab.

## Before / after (es-ES)

Before:

```
RECENT REQUESTS                     Topología del proveedor
Model      In / Out      When        0 activo · 1 error     ● Activo  ● Recent  ● error
No requests yet.
```

After:

```
SOLICITUDES RECIENTES               Topología del proveedor
Modelo     Entrada / Salida  Cuándo  0 activo · 1 error     ● Activo  ● Reciente  ● Error
Aún no hay solicitudes.
```

## Related Issues

- No open issue covers this (`gh issue list --search "recent requests i18n"` / `--search topology` return unrelated backlog items).

## Validation

- [x] Change type: i18n / UI
- [x] Focused tests and category gates from the golden path: `tests/unit/i18n-home-recent-requests-topology-legend.test.ts` 5/5; neighbouring i18n suites (`i18n-vi-completeness`, `i18n-placeholder-parity`, `i18n-ui-value-drift`, `i18n-pt-br`, `i18n-locale-surfaces-parity`, `translator-friendly-i18n-keys`, `i18n-hardcoded-ui-regressions`, `i18n-translation-ratio-gate`, `i18n-config`) 250/250; `npm run i18n:check-ui-coverage` PASS (41 locales ≥ 80%); `BASE_REF=origin/release/v3.8.51 npm run i18n:check-value-drift` PASS; `npm run i18n:check-ratio` OK (41 locales within baseline +0.5); `npm run check:changelog-integrity` OK; `node scripts/check/check-complexity-ratchets.mjs --base-ref origin/release/v3.8.51` OK (0 violations)
- [ ] `npm run lint` — not run repository-wide; eslint and prettier were run on the two touched TS files and the catalogs, both clean
- [x] Reconciled with the current active release base `release/v3.8.51`; focused checks rerun afterward
- [x] Production-code changes include a new or updated automated test in this PR
- SonarQube is temporarily opt-in while the private project has no quota; it is not a PR gate.

Red on the base: the new test file fails 4 of 5 cases against `release/v3.8.51` (keys missing, English copies present, legend borrowing `settings.recent`); green with this change (5/5).

## Tests Added Or Updated

- `tests/unit/i18n-home-recent-requests-topology-legend.test.ts` (new, 5 cases): the eight home-widget keys exist and are non-empty in all 42 catalogs; es/pt/pt-BR/fr/de/it/vi hold real translations (no `__MISSING__` marker, not the English value, with `es.home.topologyLegendError = "Error"` allow-listed as a genuine cognate); no locale keeps a silent English copy of the five recent-requests keys (translated or marked); `HomeProviderTopologySection.tsx` reads the legend from `home.topologyLegend*` and no longer from `settings.recent` / `analytics.modelStatusError`; the three legend labels share capitalisation within each maintained locale.

## Coverage Notes

- `src/app/(dashboard)/dashboard/HomeProviderTopologySection.tsx`: the only production change is three `t()` calls and the removal of three unused `useTranslations` hooks; the new static test pins the key names it must use. No touched file lost coverage.
- `src/i18n/messages/*.json`: catalog data, covered by the new test and the existing i18n gates listed above.

## Reviewer Notes

- The `__MISSING__:` markers replace values that were already English, so nothing regresses visually in those locales: `deepMergeFallback` (`src/i18n/request.ts`) renders the English fallback exactly as before. The change makes the debt visible to the translation pipeline instead of hiding it as "covered".
- `nl.home.recentRequestsModel` becomes `__MISSING__:Model` although Dutch "Model" is correct; I left it to the pipeline rather than hand-pick cognates outside the languages I can vouch for. The same applies to any other coincidental cognate among the marked locales.
- German legend "Zuletzt" (most recently routed) was chosen over "Kürzlich" because the amber dot marks the last provider that served a request, not a time window.
- Manual check on a Spanish UI: home page with `showProviderTopologyOnHome` enabled, then confirm the panel header, the three column headers, the empty state and the legend all read in Spanish, and that the legend casing matches the "Activo · Reciente · Error" row.

title: fix(orchestration): emit the real task status on non-status updates
body:
## Summary

- `updateCloudAgentTask` (`src/lib/cloudAgent/db.ts:124`) published `state: "updated"` on `agent.task.updated` whenever the update carried no `status` field. The `activities` sync in `src/app/api/v1/agents/tasks/[id]/route.ts:175` and the `result`/`error` writes hit that path, so the `agents` WS channel carried a fabricated state that no `OrchState` maps to. This is the first bullet of the PR-B1 minors in #12392 ("read the row's real `status` or document `"updated"` as a sentinel").
- The writer now reads the row's current `status` after the `UPDATE` and publishes that; a status-carrying update still publishes the value it wrote, without the extra read. When no row matched the id nothing was written, so nothing is published either (the A2A `updateTask` already behaves this way for an unknown id).
- Deliberately out of scope: the duplicated `emitAgentTaskUpdated` helper (third bullet, it needs `a2a/taskManager.ts` and lands better after PR-B2), the no-op `status` write in the GET sync (fourth bullet), and the `hubProxy` module-level state (second bullet).

## Related Issues

- Refs #12392 (PR-B1 minors, first bullet)
